turns: How does eager endpointing decide that I've finished speaking?
rows.reply: Eager endpointing watches for 200 ms of VAD silence and then asks Deepgram to finalize the transcript; if a final ending in “.”, “?” or “!” arrives while that silence is at least 200 ms, the turn ends, otherwise it falls back to the fixed 800 ms silence rule [2][3].

turns: How does the echo gate stop the agent from interrupting itself?
rows.reply: The echo gate watches the microphone while the agent is playing and only counts a frame as speech if the VAD is significantly higher than usual and the mic’s power is close to the played audio, requiring at least 160 ms of such speech before it will treat the signal as a user turn[1]. By keeping these stricter thresholds on for 200 ms after playback ends, any lingering echo from the speaker is rejected, so the recognizer never hears the agent’s own voice and the agent can’t cancel its own answer[4].

turns: What is a generation fence?
rows.reply: A generation fence is the highest generation ID that has been cancelled in a session, and it is used by every queue owner to drop any audio frames belonging to that generation or any older one. Each component— the orchestrator, the gateway’s send queue, and the browser playout—updates its fence to `max(fence, g)` when it receives an `agent.cancel{gen}` and then discards any queued or arriving frames with `generation_id <= fence` [5]. This ensures that cancelled answers never get played, even if frames were already buffered or arrive later on the network [1][3].

turns: How do I embed the voice widget on my own website?
rows.reply: You add the classic script tag `<script src=" data-endpoint=" data-title="Ask the docs"></script>` to any page, keeping the `data-` attributes on that tag so the widget can read its configuration [1]. The script mounts automatically once the page has a body (or on DOMContentLoaded if it’s in the head) and adds a launcher button in the bottom‑right corner; opening the launcher connects to the gateway [1].

turns: Where do I put my Deepgram and Cartesia keys?
rows.reply: You add your `DEEPGRAM_API_KEY` and `CARTESIA_API_KEY` to the `.env` file at the repository root (copy `.env.example` first) so the orchestrator can read them from the process environment [1]. Those keys are never sent to the browser; they stay on the server and are used only by the orchestrator [4].

turns: How long does the gateway keep my session after the connection drops?
rows.reply: The gateway holds onto a session for ten seconds after the client’s WebSocket disconnects, keeping the upstream connection to the orchestrator open during that window [1]. After those ten seconds the session expires and a new hello will start a fresh session [2].

turns: Which language model does VoiceCore use, and why that one?
rows.reply: VoiceCore uses the `openai/gpt-oss-120b` model accessed via OpenRouter and runs on Cerebras because it offers a low‑reasoning‑effort option that fits the system’s latency goals [1]. That model was selected as part of the speed improvements that cut response times dramatically, helping achieve the sub‑second latency targets [5].

turns: How do I measure latency with the benchmark runner?
rows.reply: You run the benchmark by picking the harness that matches the kind of latency you want—use the WSS runner for a real end‑to‑end measurement that includes transport and live provider delays, or the in‑process runner for a deterministic, repeatable number that only changes when the code changes [1]. Then start a live run (or a mock run) with the appropriate command, let it record traces, and finally compute the breakdown with `harness/timeline.py` as shown in the “How to reproduce a latency run” instructions [2].

turns: What fields are in the audio frame header?
rows.reply: The audio frame header consists of a 28‑byte big‑endian block with the fields `version`, `kind`, `flags`, `stream_id`, `sequence`, `capture_us`, `generation_id` and `samples` in that order [1].

turns: How does the browser SDK turn microphone audio into frames?
rows.reply: The browser SDK first asks for microphone permission and opens the mic with echo‑cancellation, noise suppression and auto‑gain control enabled[1]. It captures the raw audio in an AudioWorklet that delivers 128‑sample blocks, then resamples those blocks to 16 kHz and converts them to 16‑bit PCM[2]. A framer cuts the PCM stream into 320‑sample (20 ms) frames, adds a 28‑byte header, and sends each frame as a binary WebSocket message[3].

turns: How do I point the assistant at my own Docusaurus docs?
rows.reply: You point the assistant at your own Docusaurus docs by running the orchestrator with the `--docs-dir` flag set to the folder containing your Markdown files and the `--docs-url` flag set to the base URL where those docs are served [1][3]. The `--docs-dir` defaults to `apps/docs/docs` and `--docs-url` defaults to `, so you need to override them to match your site’s location [3].

turns: Why does VoiceCore use WebSocket instead of WebRTC?
rows.reply: VoiceCore keeps WebSocket because it lets the same binary frames and JSON events travel from the browser to the gateway and on to the orchestrator, so only one protocol is needed for both hops [1]. Using TCP means frames can’t reorder, so the gateway only needs simple bounded queues instead of a jitter buffer, and the measured extra latency is tiny [1]. WebRTC would require additional infrastructure like ICE and TURN servers, which adds complexity for only marginal benefit in lossy networks [1].

turns: What is eager endpointing?
And what if I pause in the middle of a question?
rows.reply: If you pause in the middle of a question, the eager endpoint will end the turn once the pause exceeds about 800 ms, which can cause the assistant to start answering the first half of your query [2]. However, if you resume speaking within the 2.5‑second merge window and before any answer is audible, the continuation‑merge logic will cancel that early answer and combine the two parts so the assistant answers the whole question as a single turn [5].

turns: How does barge-in work?
How fast is it?
rows.reply: Barge‑in typically silences the agent within a few hundred milliseconds after the user starts speaking; in fake‑provider runs the median (p50) interrupt‑to‑silence is about 180 ms with no network delay and rises to roughly 380 ms with 100 ms one‑way delay [3]. In live runs the median is around 303 ms, though occasional clips can take longer due to short initial words or processing lag [3][5].
